passage: Four days after the breakup, Jatin had an internal exam and a hostel room he shared with Ramesh, who liked music at night. There was no quiet corner to fall apart in. On the first night Jatin kept scrolling through old photos until Ramesh gently took the phone and set it face down. 'Revise one chapter, then you can be sad for ten minutes. Deal?' Jatin laughed despite himself. He muted her chats instead of deleting them; he could decide about that later. Then he wrote down, honestly, what had not worked: she wanted to move abroad, he wanted to stay near his parents, and neither of them was wrong. The exam went average. That evening he called his sister, ate a proper dinner, and slept before midnight for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do when Jatin kept scrolling through old photos?
qa.a: Ramesh gently took the phone, set it face down and offered a deal: revise one chapter, then be sad for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Jatin mute her chats instead of deleting them?
qa.a: He was still hurting and not ready to make a final decision, so muting gave him distance without forcing a choice he might regret.

qa.q: What helped Jatin get through that week despite the exam pressure?
qa.a: Small structure did: short study blocks, naming honestly why they did not fit, eating, sleeping and calling his sister. He could keep leaning on people instead of old photos.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Ramesh's part in that week?
qa.a: Ramesh probably knew the heartbreak could not be fixed, but a light joke and a bit of structure could keep Jatin steady 🙂

grounding: Shows recovering from a breakup under exam pressure by understanding the value mismatch and rebuilding routines with a friend's help.

passage: Arnab was funny, and on their third coffee at the café near Gariahat, Gopika laughed more than she had in weeks. Then the waiter brought the wrong order, and Arnab snapped his fingers at him and said something sharp. Later, when she mentioned her plan to teach at a night school on weekends, he called it 'cute timepass'. On the auto ride home she made a list in her notes: kind to strangers, takes my work seriously, honest. He had one out of three. The next day she texted him that she had enjoyed talking but didn't feel they wanted the same things. He replied, 'Fair. Bit of a blow, honestly, but thanks for saying it straight.' She read it twice, a little sad, and a little proud of herself.

qa.q: Where did Gopika and Arnab have their third coffee?
qa.a: At the café near Gariahat.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling after reading Arnab's reply?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: a little sad to close something fun, and proud that she chose by what mattered to her rather than by the laughter alone.

qa.q: How did Gopika's list help her decide?
qa.a: It turned a vague uneasy feeling into clear values, kindness, respect for her work and honesty, so her choice was not based only on chemistry.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt receiving her text?
qa.a: Stung, since he admits it was a blow, but he chose to respect her honesty instead of arguing, which let both of them move on with dignity.

grounding: Illustrates choosing a partner by values and both people handling a rejection honestly.

passage: Monday: Walking back from class, Yamini told Ramesh she wasn't ready to stay over at his flat. He went quiet, kicked a pebble, then said, 'Okay. Thanks for telling me straight instead of making an excuse.' Thursday: On the sofa watching a film while his flatmates were out, he paused before sliding closer. 'This fine?' She nodded, then added that kissing was fine but she wanted to stop there for now. He said, 'Then that's where we stop.' Later they talked, a bit awkwardly, about how any bigger step would come with a real conversation first and proper protection, and how a clinic visit together would not be embarrassing. The next Sunday: Yamini told her roommate she felt safer with Ramesh than with anyone before. 'He asks. And he listens when I answer.'

qa.q: What did Ramesh ask on Thursday before moving closer?
qa.a: He paused and asked, 'This fine?'

qa.q: How can you tell Ramesh felt disappointed on Monday but still chose respect?
qa.a: He went quiet and kicked a pebble, which hints at disappointment, yet he thanked her for being honest instead of pushing.

qa.q: What made their talk about bigger steps a responsible one?
qa.a: They agreed any bigger step needs a real conversation first and proper protection, and that seeing a clinic together is nothing to be ashamed of, so both stay informed and safe.

qa.q: What would change for Yamini if Ramesh had argued on Monday?
qa.a: She might have felt pressured and less safe saying no later; his respect is what built the trust she describes on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a couple communicating boundaries, checking consent and planning responsibly, with trust growing over several days.

passage: Tushar, sit. You asked why I keep telling you boys to ask properly. When I was twenty-one, in Nagpur, I liked a girl from my college drama group. One evening after rehearsal I leaned in to kiss her, sure she wanted it because she'd been laughing at my jokes all week. She stepped back. Just one step. My face burned, and for a second I wanted to be angry, as if she owed me something. Luckily my mouth said, 'Sorry, I should have asked.' She looked relieved and said, 'I like you. Just slower.' We stayed friends for years. Laughing at a joke is not a yes, beta. A step back is a no. And whatever happens later in your life, you both talk first and keep each other safe.

qa.q: Where was the narrator studying when this happened?
qa.a: In Nagpur, as part of a college drama group.

qa.q: What did the narrator feel when the girl stepped back?
qa.a: Embarrassment, with a burning face, and a brief flash of anger as if she owed something, before choosing to apologise.

qa.q: What does the narrator want Tushar to take away from the story?
qa.a: That friendliness or laughter is not consent; Tushar should ask, treat a step back as a no, and talk openly before any intimacy.

qa.q: How might the girl have experienced the narrator's apology?
qa.a: She was relieved; the quick sorry showed her that her boundary was safe, which is why she could say she liked the narrator but wanted things slower.

grounding: An elder recalls learning at twenty-one that consent must be asked for and a boundary respected.

passage: First week of June: Kashish's father, Sachin, called three times a day from Indore, asking what she had eaten and why she hadn't come home that weekend. On the third call she snapped, 'Papa, I'm not ten!' and hung up, then felt awful. Ten days later: She called him on her own, calmly. 'I miss you too. Can we do one long call every Sunday, and I'll come home alternate weekends? The daily check-ins make me feel watched.' Papa was silent, then said, 'Your mother said you would say this.' He sounded hurt, but he agreed. Early July: On their Sunday call he asked what she thought about him taking early retirement. She listened, asked questions and gave her view. After hanging up she realised he had never asked her opinion like that before.

qa.q: How often did Sachin call Kashish in the first week of June?
qa.a: Three times a day, from Indore.

qa.q: Why did Kashish feel awful after snapping at her father?
qa.a: She loved him and knew he called out of care, so hanging up felt unfair even though the calls made her feel watched.

qa.q: What worked about the way Kashish set her boundary the second time?
qa.a: She called calmly, said she missed him too and offered a concrete plan, Sunday calls and alternate weekends, so it felt like a new arrangement rather than rejection.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when he asked Kashish about early retirement?
qa.a: He was starting to treat her as an adult he could consult; after the hurt of her boundary, that may have felt strange but also closer.

grounding: Shows a young adult replacing constant parental check-ins with a calm boundary, and the relationship becoming more of an adult partnership.

passage: Avni mol, you think your Amma is strict about your hostel curfew? When I left Thrissur for my first job in Chennai at twenty, my own Amma sent a letter every week listing whom I should avoid. I read them and felt like a small boy again. For months I wrote back only 'All fine.' Then my first salary came. I sent her some money and a proper letter, about my work, my roommate, a mistake I made with my boss and how I fixed it. I asked her advice about one thing only: how to cook her fish curry. Her next letter had no warnings. Just the recipe, and one line: 'Jomon, you manage your life well.' Telling her more, not less, is what helped her let go, mol.

qa.q: Where did Jomon move for his first job?
qa.a: From Thrissur to Chennai, when he was twenty.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel reading his mother's weekly letters?
qa.a: They made him feel like a small boy again, watched rather than trusted, so he sent back short 'All fine' replies.

qa.q: According to Jomon, what changed the relationship with his mother?
qa.a: Sharing real details of his life, including a mistake and how he fixed it, and asking her advice on something small showed her he was capable and still valued her.

qa.q: How might Jomon's mother have felt when the fuller letter arrived?
qa.a: Reassured; seeing how he handled problems let her worry less and trust him, as her line 'you manage your life well' shows.

grounding: An elder recalls moving from dependence to an adult relationship with his mother through openness rather than distance.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 pm
Sabina's voice note came at lunch, seven minutes long, about her new lab in Pune and a landlady who hums film songs at 6 am. I listened in two parts between classes and grinned like an idiot. Then I realised I hadn't replied to her last one for nine days. Nine! Not because I don't care. Just placements, assignments, laundry, sleep. Scary how easily a four-year friendship turns into 'haha same' replies. So tonight I sent a real one back, and we fixed a thing: every second Saturday, a call while we both cook dinner, no cancelling unless someone is sick. She said, 'Deal, Karthik, and you have to show me your terrible sambar.' Wrote it in my planner in red. Friendships apparently need calendar slots now. Fine. She's worth a slot.

qa.q: What did Karthik and Sabina agree to do every second Saturday?
qa.a: Have a call while they both cook dinner, with no cancelling unless someone is sick.

qa.q: What worried Karthik on realising there had been no reply for nine days?
qa.a: Karthik was scared their four-year friendship could shrink into shallow 'haha same' replies because of busyness, not lack of care.

qa.q: Why does a fixed slot help a friendship like this?
qa.a: It stops the friendship depending on spare time, which busy weeks rarely have; a regular, easy ritual like cooking together keeps it going.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt getting Karthik's real reply after nine days?
qa.a: Probably relieved and valued; her teasing about Karthik's sambar suggests she was glad to be back to their easy closeness 😊

grounding: Shows keeping a long friendship alive across cities and busy schedules by setting up a regular shared ritual.

passage:
Rekha: u alive?? last msg from you was 3 weeks ago 😅
Simran: barely. new internship + evening classes. I'm so sorry
Rekha: not a guilt trip. I just miss you
Simran: miss you too. honestly I keep thinking I'll call when I have a free hour and that hour never comes

Simran: bus at 8:15!

Rekha: especially then

Rekha: writing it in pen 🎉
Simran: ❤️

qa.q: What did Rekha mean when Rekha said 'not a guilt trip'?

qa.q: Why is the commute call a good plan?
qa.a: It uses time they already have instead of waiting for a free hour that never comes, and it is short enough to keep up in busy weeks.

passage: Week one: Tejas ate dinner in his room in Hyderabad, watching videos of home, the ghats on the Brahmaputra, his mother's kitchen. The mess felt too loud. On the phone he told his mother he was fine. Week three: Hrithik from the next room knocked to borrow an extension board and noticed the guitar under the bed. 'You play? A few of us jam on the terrace on Fridays.' Tejas said maybe, then spent Friday evening almost not going. He went for twenty minutes, mostly listening. Week seven: Tejas carried the guitar up himself, taught two people a Bihu rhythm, and afterwards ate in the mess with them, arguing about biryani. He still missed home on some nights. But now he also had somewhere to be on Fridays.

qa.q: What did Hrithik notice when he came to borrow an extension board?
qa.a: The guitar under Tejas's bed.

qa.q: Why did Tejas tell his mother he was fine in week one?
qa.a: Probably so she would not worry, even though he was lonely and spending his evenings watching videos of home.

qa.q: What small step helped Tejas most?
qa.a: Going to the terrace jam for just twenty minutes, even only to listen; a small, low-pressure start made later belonging possible.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the invitation?
qa.a: To Hrithik it may have been a casual offer while borrowing something, without knowing how much it would matter to someone new and far from home.

grounding: Shows loneliness after moving to a new campus easing over weeks as the student builds belonging through a shared activity.

passage: Vaibhav, you keep saying everyone in Pune already has friends. Let me tell you about my first year in Delhi, at nineteen. I came from a small town near Jabalpur, and I cried in the hostel bathroom so no one would hear. I wrote long letters home saying the food was bad and the girls were snobbish. Really, I was just afraid to speak first. What changed it was silly. The warden needed volunteers to decorate for Diwali, and I was good with rangoli. I knelt on that floor for two evenings with four strangers, sharing colours. By the end, one of them, Farah, had become my friend, and her room became my second home. The ache for home doesn't vanish, beta. You just build a second place to miss.

qa.q: What did the narrator volunteer to do in the first year in Delhi?
qa.a: Decorate the hostel for Diwali by making rangoli.

qa.q: What was the narrator really feeling behind the complaints in the letters home?
qa.a: The narrator admits being afraid to speak first; calling the girls snobbish covered that fear and loneliness.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav try in Pune, based on this story?
qa.a: Vaibhav could join one shared task or activity where working side by side makes talking easier, instead of waiting to be approached.

qa.q: How might Farah have seen the narrator during those evenings?
qa.a: Probably just as a quiet newcomer good at rangoli; Farah would not know about the crying alone, which shows how hidden loneliness can be.

grounding: An elder recalls building belonging after moving away from home for college, to encourage a lonely younger person.

passage: I share the flat in Andheri with Ritu and Zubin, so I had a front-row seat. The electricity bill had jumped, and Ritu kept glancing at Zubin's gaming setup, which ran most nights. For a week she said nothing and just stacked his unwashed pans pointedly by the sink. I couldn't tell if she was angry or just tired. Then on Sunday she put the bill on the table and asked if we could sit for ten minutes. She didn't accuse him. She suggested splitting the base amount equally and Zubin paying a bit extra for the months he games a lot. Zubin looked defensive at first, arms crossed, then shrugged. 'Fair. Can we also do a dishes chart? I'm bad at noticing.' The chart is still on the fridge, slightly crooked.

qa.q: In which area is the flat the narrator shares with Ritu and Zubin?
qa.a: In Andheri.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling during the week she stayed silent?
qa.a: The narrator could not be sure, but stacking the pans pointedly suggests frustration building up that she had not yet put into words.

qa.q: Why did Sunday's conversation work better than the silent pans?
qa.a: Ritu chose a calm time, used the bill as a shared fact and proposed a fair split instead of blaming, so Zubin could agree and add his own idea.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt when Ritu put the bill on the table?
qa.a: Defensive at first, as his crossed arms show, but her calm offer let him admit he is bad at noticing and help fix it.

grounding: A flatmate observes roommates settling a money and chores conflict fairly after a tense week.

passage: Day 1: Salma found her milk finished again and a note in Kiran's handwriting: 'Sorry! Will replace.' It was the fourth note that month. She typed a long angry message, deleted it, and left for college, jaw tight all day. Day 4: Over chai in their PG kitchen in Kochi, Salma said, 'I like living with you, but the borrowing is costing me money and patience.' Kiran went red. 'I thought the notes made it okay.' They agreed on a shared jar for milk, bread and oil, each putting in the same amount every Monday, with personal things on separate shelves. Day 20: The jar ran low, and Kiran topped it up without being asked, adding a packet of Salma's favourite biscuits. Salma laughed and stuck a note on it: 'Forgiven, twice over.'

qa.q: Which items did the shared jar cover?
qa.a: Milk, bread and oil, with each of them putting in the same amount every Monday.

qa.q: Why did Salma delete her long angry message?
qa.a: She was upset but seemed not to want a written fight to damage a friendship she valued, so she waited to talk calmly in person.

qa.q: What made their agreement fair?
qa.a: Shared basics were paid for equally and personal things stayed on separate shelves, so neither had to track small debts or feel taken for granted.

qa.q: How did Kiran see the borrowing before Day 4?
qa.a: Kiran genuinely thought the 'Sorry! Will replace' notes made it okay and did not realise what it was costing Salma.

grounding: Shows roommates moving from silent resentment to a fair shared-money system over three weeks.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: So, Vaibhav, you asked how I knew it wasn't just a bad week. Honestly, I didn't, not at first. Third year, I was sleeping ten hours and still waking up tired. I stopped going to badminton, which I love. My roommate would ask about dinner and I'd say 'later' till the mess closed. The scary bit was this flat feeling, like nothing I did would matter anyway. It went on and on. What finally moved me was my younger cousin on a video call asking, 'Yamini didi, why don't you laugh anymore?' The next day I booked a slot with the campus counsellor. My hands were shaking in the waiting room. She didn't fix everything in one session, but she took it seriously, and we made a plan that included seeing a doctor too. I wish I'd gone earlier.

qa.q: Which sport did Yamini stop going to?
qa.a: Badminton, which she loves.

qa.q: Why did the flat feeling scare Yamini?
qa.a: It felt like nothing she did would matter anyway; that hopelessness scared her more than the tiredness because it was so unlike her.

qa.q: What does Yamini's story suggest about when to seek help?
qa.a: When exhaustion, withdrawal or hopelessness keep going and do not lift, reaching a counsellor or doctor early helps; she wishes she had not waited 🙏

qa.q: What might it have been like for her cousin to notice she didn't laugh anymore?
qa.a: The cousin probably missed the old Yamini and felt puzzled or worried, and that simple question made the change visible to Yamini herself.

grounding: A student tells a friend how she noticed lasting exhaustion, withdrawal and hopelessness and sought professional help.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: I'm Mohit, Divyansh's roommate since first year. Something shifted around October. He stopped coming to the canteen with us, left assignments half done, and his lamp stayed off even when he was clearly awake. When I joked that he was becoming a monk, he didn't even smile. I wasn't sure what was going on, maybe exams, maybe home. I didn't want to be dramatic. But after a few weeks I sat on the edge of his bed and said, 'You seem really low, and I'm worried. Not judging.' He shrugged and said he was just tired all the time and didn't see the point of much. I told him about the student wellness centre and offered to walk there with him. He said no. Two days later he asked, 'Does that offer still stand?' It did.

qa.q: When did Mohit notice something shift in Divyansh?
qa.a: Around October.

qa.q: Why did Mohit hesitate before saying anything?
qa.a: Mohit was not sure what was going on and worried about seeming dramatic or intrusive.

qa.q: Which part of Mohit's approach helped, and why?
qa.a: He named his worry without judging and made help concrete by offering to walk to the wellness centre with him, then left the door open after a no.

qa.q: How might things have gone if Mohit had kept joking instead of asking?
qa.a: Divyansh might have stayed hidden behind being 'just tired', and the warning signs could have gone unaddressed for much longer.

grounding: A roommate notices signs of withdrawal and hopelessness and gently helps a friend toward professional support.

passage:
Friday night
Lost again. Not a huge amount, but it was my mess money for the month, and I only meant to play 'one round' of that online card game after dinner. I keep doing the same thing: lose, feel sick, play again to win it back, win a little, feel great, play more. It's a loop and I'm the hamster in the wheel. Tarun saw me on my phone at 2 am last week and asked if I was okay. I lied and said I was chatting. Today I told him the truth. He didn't lecture. He just said, 'Let's deal with it, Nilesh.' So: uninstalled the app, gave Tarun my debit card to keep for now, and tomorrow I'm calling Maa, even though I'm dreading it. Tarun also found a helpline for gambling problems. I saved the number. Scared. Also lighter.

qa.q: What money did Nilesh lose?
qa.a: The mess money for the month.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Scared and lighter at once; Nilesh dreads calling Maa, yet telling Tarun and taking steps has eased the weight of the secret.

qa.q: Which steps help Nilesh break the loop?
qa.a: Removing the app, putting the debit card out of easy reach, planning to tell family and saving a helpline number give barriers and support instead of willpower alone.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh told him the truth?
qa.a: Perhaps a little hurt about the earlier lie, but mostly concerned and glad to be trusted, which is why he said, 'Let's deal with it.' 🤍

grounding: A diary entry shows a student recognising a gambling dependence loop and taking first steps to exit it with support.

passage:
Dear Sachin,
You asked on the phone why I turned down the internship shortcut that half our batch took, where you pay a middleman for a certificate without doing the work. I didn't explain well, so here goes. Papa thinks I'm foolish for losing a line on my CV. Some of our friends think I'm acting superior. I've thought about it for weeks, and I keep landing in the same place: I don't want anything with my name on it that isn't true. That's my line, not Papa's or the group's. I'm also realising I care about work that helps someone real, which is why I'm volunteering at the literacy centre instead. I'm not judging you. I just needed you to know it's a choice, not stubbornness.
Still your friend,
Kashish

qa.q: Where is Kashish volunteering instead of taking the shortcut?
qa.a: At the literacy centre.

qa.q: What does Kashish want Sachin to understand?
qa.a: That the refusal comes from Kashish's own settled value of honesty, not stubbornness or feeling superior, and that the friendship still matters.

qa.q: How did Kashish reach this decision?
qa.a: Kashish thought about it for weeks and kept landing on the same principle, which helped separate Kashish's own line from Papa's and the group's opinions.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Maybe a little defensive, since Sachin may have taken the shortcut too, but the line 'I'm not judging you' can help Sachin see it as Kashish's choice rather than an attack.

grounding: A letter shows a young adult naming a personal non-negotiable of honesty even when family and peers disagree.

passage: Mridul, you want the honest version for your campus radio show? Okay. In second year, the seniors in my hostel expected us to 'welcome' the freshers: make them sing at midnight, stand on chairs, that sort of thing. My uncle, who studied there too, had told me it builds character. Everyone laughed like it was tradition. I stood there watching a skinny kid from Siliguri shaking on a chair, and something in me just said no. Not loudly. I walked him back to his room and told him he didn't have to come out again. The seniors called me soft for months. What I figured out that year is that I care about people not being humiliated, even when the whole room finds it funny. That's mine now. Nobody handed it to me.

qa.q: What had the narrator's uncle said about the tradition?
qa.a: That it builds character.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling while watching the fresher on the chair?
qa.a: Uneasy and protective; seeing the boy shaking made something in the narrator refuse to go along with it.

qa.q: What could someone in the narrator's position do if they fear standing out?
qa.a: Quiet action still counts: walking the person away, telling them they do not have to go back, and finding one or two people who share the value makes it easier to hold.

qa.q: How might the fresher from Siliguri remember that night?
qa.a: Probably with huge relief that one senior treated him with dignity, which may shape how he treats juniors later.

grounding: A student tells how they chose their own value of dignity over a hostel tradition backed by seniors and family.

passage: Monday: Gargi saw 'Fail' next to her accounts paper and walked straight to the library washroom. You're useless. Everyone else managed. Why do you even try? She didn't eat lunch. Wednesday: Neelam found her staring at the result on her phone. 'What would you say to me if these were my marks?' Gargi thought about it. 'That one paper isn't the whole degree. That I should see where I lost marks.' Neelam just raised an eyebrow. Gargi sighed. 'Okay. Same to me, then.' Two weeks later: Studying for the re-exam, Gargi caught herself muttering 'idiot' after a wrong answer. She stopped, took a breath and wrote in the margin: Mistake in step two again. Slow down. You can learn this. She redid the problem, and got it right.

qa.q: Which paper did Gargi fail?
qa.a: Her accounts paper.

qa.q: What does Gargi's inner voice on Monday reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: She was treating herself harshly, calling herself useless and comparing herself to everyone, and was too upset even to eat.

qa.q: How did Neelam's question help?
qa.a: By asking what Gargi would say to a friend, it let Gargi find kinder, practical words herself instead of being told what to think.

qa.q: If Neelam had just said 'Don't worry, it's fine', what might have changed?
qa.a: Gargi might have felt brushed off and kept her harsh self-talk, without finding the accountable plan she later wrote in the margin.

grounding: Shows a student replacing harsh self-criticism after a failed paper with kind but accountable self-talk over two weeks.

passage: Payal, stop apologising and sit a minute. You think one wrong entry makes you a disaster? At twenty-two, in my first month at this very branch, I sent a customer's cheque to the wrong account. My manager caught it before any harm was done, but I went home and replayed it all night, calling myself every name. Next morning I was so frightened I nearly didn't come in. My father made tea and asked, 'Indu, what did you learn?' I said, 'To double-check the account number before stamping.' He said, 'Then that's what you take back. Leave the insults at home.' I went in, owned the mistake to my manager, and made myself a checklist. I still use it. See? Owning it and being kind to yourself can go together.

qa.q: What mistake did Indu make in the first month at the branch?
qa.a: Indu sent a customer's cheque to the wrong account.

qa.q: How did Indu feel the night after the mistake?
qa.a: Ashamed and frightened; Indu replayed it all night, called themselves names and almost did not go to work the next morning.

qa.q: What could Payal take from Indu's story?
qa.a: Payal can own the wrong entry, turn the lesson into a checklist and drop the self-insults, since a clear fix helps more than harshness.

qa.q: How might Payal feel hearing a senior share this?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, seeing that a respected senior made a similar mistake and grew from it 😊

grounding: A senior colleague recalls learning to own a mistake while being kind to oneself, to reassure a young trainee.
